summary:
### Key Topics Discussed
- Weekly planning and optimization of tasks.
- Definition of personal time/schedule for performers or teams.
- Integration of fixed meal breaks and rest periods into the weekly schedule.
- Dynamic planning based on estimated task times and desired delivery times.
- Prioritization of personal time vs. planned tasks using time codes.
- Classification of time codes for follow-up, salary reports, and economic/statistical analysis.
- Creation of tasks with production time codes and high priority, leading to rough and fine planning.
- Coordination of performer's self-scheduled personal time, created via an editor.
- Personal time definition using a "light order concept" with start/end times and repetition capabilities.
- Overview of three main time types in time planning: production time, setup time (travel/preparation), and personal time (egentid).
- Two primary time groups: production time (money-generating) and setup time (non-productive, e.g., travel or vehicle preparation).
- Route optimization for weekly task planning based on location.
- AI-supported electronic optimization vs. manual planning by the planner or performer.
- System warnings for maintaining delivery time windows if tasks are misplaced.
- Automatic calculation of travel time by the system between tasks and to/from rest locations.
- Adjustment of time codes, such as for initial travel to a work location.
- Classification of initial travel to work (e.g., Sundsvall from Ariavägen 2 in Bjästa) as personal time (egentid) despite being a travel to setup work.

### Decisions Made
- No decisions were made.

### Action Items
- Need to develop a concept for defining personal time within the weekly schedule.
- Develop a function, similar to the order concept, for performers to schedule recurring fixed meal breaks (e.g., Monday-Friday, 12:00-12:45).
- Enable performers to plan their night rest and weekend rest within the system.
- The system should repeat these scheduled times weekly and annually.
- Implement a side register to define time codes with priority levels.

### Important Points & Insights
- The importance of grouping tasks by address for weekly scheduling.
- Route optimization will be a key component of the planning process.
- The system must accommodate and respect pre-defined personal times like meal breaks and rest periods.
- Planned jobs are rough estimations against desired delivery times, requiring a dynamic system.
- Personal time (egentid) will have lower priority and must be able to be overridden or rescheduled if necessary, for example, if scheduled for weekend rest but jobs are in Sundsvall.
- Time codes for production and travel time will have high priority.
- Time codes for internal time and personal time will have lower priority.
- The system will use time codes and their priorities to manage task shifts and overlaps.
- Personal time with a high priority code (e.g., doctor's appointment) will have the same priority as a job, preventing overbooking.
- Time codes are primarily for tracking employee time, generating salary reports, and for economic/statistical follow-up.
- Tasks, such as washing ten vessels, will be created with production time codes and high priority, then placed in rough and fine planning.
- Personal time will be created using an editor and will be integrated into the performer's planning.
- The concept of personal time scheduling is similar to a simplified order concept, allowing for start/end times and repetition.
- There are three overarching time types within the time planning view: production time, setup time (travel/preparation), and personal time.
- Production time is defined as money-generating and part of the employee's working hours, including travel between tasks within the same location.
- Setup time, such as general travel or preparing a vehicle (e.g., emptying for two hours), is non-productive and not a source of income for the company, but is important to track for reduction opportunities.
- Non-productive time (e.g., travel or setup) will be automatically generated by the system, or can be defined for specific tasks.
- The system will implement route optimization for weekly planning, accounting for optimized travel routes between tasks (e.g., Storgatan 22 then Storgatan 18).
- The system, Trivo, must warn if a job is scheduled on a day when it cannot be done due to delivery deadlines or other constraints.
- Fine planning will involve puzzling together jobs, personal time, and travel for optimal scheduling.
- Travel time will be calculated automatically by the system between addresses (e.g., Storgatan 22 to Storgatan 24) and between production jobs.
- The system will calculate initial travel time to the first job of the day (e.g., from a rest location like Ariavägen 2 in Bjästa to Storgatan 22 in Sundsvall).
- There is a need to be able to adjust these time codes.
- Initial travel to the job site (e.g., to Sundsvall from Ariavägen 2 in Bjästa) should be classified as personal time, not working time, according to Swedish practice.
- The system needs to differentiate between three main time groups: personal time (egentid), production time (money-generating activities), and setup time (primarily travel for setup or other non-billable preparatory tasks).

### Open Questions/Pending Items
- How to integrate personal time definition into the weekly schedule.
- How to handle potential conflicts where personal time needs to be overridden by job requirements.
- The exact number of priority levels needed for time codes (more than two might be possible).
